document.title: Terrorism: U.S. Response to Bombings in Kenya and Tanzania: A New Policy Direction?
document.authors: Raphael F. Perl, Congressional Research Service
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Terrorism and U.S. Policy
document.note: [Unclassified] After the August 1998 embassy bombings, the U.S. struck training bases and infrastructure in Afghanistan used by groups affiliated with Usama bin Ladin and a plant in Sudan. The report says these were the first unreservedly acknowledged preemptive strikes on a terrorist network. It examines whether this is a new policy direction and the issues raised: preparedness, loss of life and civil liberties.

events.description: Bombings of the U.S. Embassies in Kenya and Tanzania; at least 252 killed (12 U.S. citizens) and over 5,000 injured.
U.S. retaliatory and preemptive missile strikes on training bases in Afghanistan and a pharmaceutical plant in Sudan.
President signed E.O. 13099 freezing assets of bin Laden, specific associates and the Islamic Army Organization.
Federal grand jury in New York indicted bin Laden (reported 25 Aug 1998) in connection with earlier terrorist acts in the U.S.
Bombing of a Planet Hollywood restaurant in Capetown killed one and wounded 24, termed a 'retaliatory' bombing.
Sandy Berger briefed Lott and Gingrich; Gephardt's office briefed; Daschle briefed the next day.
Cohen, Albright, Tenet and Shelton met with Senators and available House Members to discuss the strikes' planning and rationale.
U.S. bombing of Libya after the Berlin Disco bombing.
U.S. bombing of Iraq in response to a plot to assassinate former President Bush.
Sharm al-Sheikh peacemaker/terrorism summit.
First acknowledged preemptive U.S. strikes against a terrorist network at multiple targets in more than one foreign nation, including a facility in Sudan characterized as a longer-term danger.

key_claims: The 20 Aug 1998 strikes on Afghan training bases and a Sudanese plant were the first acknowledged U.S. preemptive military strike against a terrorist network.
U.S. officials said they had convincing evidence that bin Laden was a major player in the 7 Aug 1998 embassy bombings.
Bin Laden's network and groups affiliated with it used training bases in Afghanistan, where the Taliban harbor him.
The Sudanese plant was identified by U.S. intelligence as a precursor chemical weapons facility with connections to bin Laden.
The report argues the Taliban's harboring of bin Laden could justify placing Afghanistan on the state sponsors of terrorism list.
The report suggests focusing publicly on individuals like bin Laden can glamorize them and attract funding and recruits, and that private funding becomes critical as state sponsorship dries up.
